title: American Investors Pour $3.4 Billion Into IPL as Two Franchise Deals Reshape Indian Cricket's Global Footprint
excerpt: Blackstone, Bolt Ventures and Walmart-backed consortiums acquired Royal Challengers Bengaluru and Rajasthan Royals in separate billion-dollar deals that signal Wall Street's growing appetite for cricket.
body:
• Royal Challengers Bengaluru sold for $1.78 billion to a consortium including Aditya Birla Group, Times of India Group, David Blitzer's Bolt Ventures and Blackstone — making it the most expensive IPL franchise transaction ever.
  • Rajasthan Royals sold for $1.63 billion to a Kal Somani-led consortium that includes Walmart, acquiring a full 100 percent stake from UK-based Emerging Media.
  • The combined $3.4 billion in deals validates IPL franchise valuations in the $1.5–2.0 billion range, according to analysts, as the league's total value crosses $10.9 billion.
  • American involvement in Indian cricket is accelerating: from Major League Cricket in the US to IPL ownership, Wall Street and Silicon Valley are betting that cricket can become a global media product.

Two separate billion-dollar deals have brought American capital deeper into Indian cricket than ever before, with the sales of Royal Challengers Bengaluru and Rajasthan Royals to US-backed consortiums reshaping the ownership landscape of the Indian Premier League.

RCB, the defending IPL champion and one of the league's most popular franchises, was acquired for nearly $1.78 billion by a group comprising India's Aditya Birla Group, The Times of India Group, David Blitzer's Bolt Ventures and American asset management giant Blackstone. The deal, which includes RCB's Women's Premier League team, makes it the most expensive franchise transaction in IPL history.

Two Deals, One Signal

Days later, Rajasthan Royals changed hands for $1.63 billion. Arizona-based investor Kal Somani, an existing minority shareholder, led a consortium that includes retail giant Walmart to acquire a full 100 percent stake from UK-based Manoj Badale's Emerging Media. Somani, in his fifties, is a serial entrepreneur with interests spanning academics and sport — he co-founded Motor City Golf Club, which has ties to Tiger Woods.

Times Group, which is part of the RCB consortium, also bid for the Royals but finished second. The BCCI, which must approve the transaction, is entitled to five percent of the sale price — roughly ₹765 crore.

"The acquisition of Rajasthan Royals by a Kal Somani-led consortium at $1.63 billion reinforces our view that IPL franchises are now valued in the $1.5–2.0 billion range, supported by strong media monetisation and rising global investor interest."

— Karan Turani, Elara Capital

Why Wall Street Wants Cricket

The IPL was recently valued at $10.9 billion by D and P Advisory, a 75 percent jump from the previous year. Media rights alone sold for $6.2 billion in the last cycle — a threefold increase over 2017 — and the combined viewership across television and streaming hit 426 million last season.

For American investors, the attraction is straightforward: cricket is the world's second-most-watched sport, and the IPL is its most commercially advanced league. Blackstone and Blitzer bring experience scaling sports properties in the US and Europe. Walmart's involvement through the Royals deal signals that the world's largest retailer sees commercial opportunity in cricket's global audience.

The deals also build on a pattern. American capital already powers Major League Cricket in the US, where Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella's group invested $16 million in the league's central equity and secured the Seattle franchise. Silicon Valley entrepreneurs, including Washington Freedom owner Sanjay Govil, have bought into England's The Hundred. IPL owners of Mumbai Indians, Lucknow SuperGiants, SunRisers Hyderabad and Delhi Capitals have also invested in Hundred teams.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, these deals matter beyond the boardroom. The IPL is the cultural Super Bowl for millions of Indians abroad, and American ownership could accelerate the league's expansion into US broadcasting and live events. With MLC building cricket stadiums in Seattle, Los Angeles and the San Francisco Bay Area, and IPL franchises now backed by US institutional capital, the sport's footprint in America is growing from a niche diaspora pastime into something closer to mainstream entertainment.

Aryaman Vikram Birla, the new RCB chairman, said the IPL "has morphed to become a global sporting powerhouse that has changed the face of Indian cricket, creating enormous value for India." Kumar Mangalam Birla, chairman of Aditya Birla Group, described the acquisition as a platform to extend the group's "legacy of institution-building into the arena of global sport."

What's Next

Both deals are subject to BCCI approval. The Somani consortium is expected to take control of the Royals after the 2026 season. Industry experts are now watching whether these valuations trigger further ownership changes among the remaining eight IPL franchises. With media rights due for renegotiation in 2027, the stakes are only getting higher. The next cycle could push IPL media rights past $10 billion — and American investors want a seat at the table.
